references.text: Moses uses the same argument about his lack of eloquence when he was first called by God at the burning bush, describing himself as slow of speech and tongue.
Moses expresses doubt that anyone will listen to him, the same concern he repeats here before Pharaoh.
Earlier in the same chapter, Moses uses exactly the same expression 'uncircumcised lips' (עֲרַל שְׂפָתַיִם) as an objection against speaking to Pharaoh.
Isaiah describes himself as a man with unclean lips when he meets God, a similar recognition of inadequacy in speech.
After Isaiah's lips were cleansed, he responded to God's call, unlike Moses' continued resistance.
God's response to Moses' objection: Aaron will be Moses' spokesman before Pharaoh.
God's response to Moses' doubt: Pharaoh's resistance is part of God's plan to harden the heart and display signs.
The fulfillment of the fear: Pharaoh does not listen, not because of Moses' speaking ability, but because his heart is hardened.
Awareness in action: Moses acts despite the fear of not being heard, yet delivers the message anyway.
Theological explanation of the problem: Pharaoh does not listen because his heart is hardened, not due to Moses' speaking ability.
God's command to act: Stand up and speak despite the fear of not being heard.
Prophetic precursor: God warns early on that Pharaoh's heart will be made hard, which answers Moses' doubt.
God's response to the doubt: Regardless of Moses' speaking ability, God's strong hand will force Pharaoh to let the people go.
